extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy; scholars studying sovereignty, succession, and civil liberty
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes normative rules and principles about forms of sovereign power, succession, types of dominion (paternal and despotic), and the nature and limits of subjects' liberty from a classical political-theory text (Hobbes, Leviathan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three kinds of sovereignty: Monarchie (one man), Democracie (the general assembly of subjects), and Aristocracie (an assembly of certain persons distinguished from the rest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixed or hybrid forms may appear in practice (elective kingdoms, limited kings, provinces governed by presidents under another state's assembly) but are to be reduced to one of these three: elective or limited kings are not sovereign in propriety but ministers of the true sovereign; provinces subject to another commonwealth are governed monarchically. Examples and clarifications about assemblies, elective kings, and limited kings are given to show how forms that look mixed are classified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elective/limited kings are ministers unless they can appoint successor
rubrics_metrics.description: An Elective King or a king with limited power is not sovereign in propriety but is a minister of the sovereign (the assembly or persons who hold the right).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an elected king has the right to appoint his successor he effectively converts election into heredity and thereby has sovereign authority; if he lacks power to appoint a successor, the sovereignty remains in whoever has the right to give it (an assembly), not in the king.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of succession vests in the present sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: The disposing of succession is, by natural right and for the conservation of peace, to be in the present sovereign; if placed in another private person or left to a dissolved multitude, the sovereign right reverts to the present possessor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no order is taken for succession, the commonwealth dissolves into war. Therefore, by institution of monarchy the present possessor is left the judgment and will to appoint a successor; otherwise the multitude is exposed to confusion and civil war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession passes by express words or testament
rubrics_metrics.description: Succession passes by express words or testament when the monarch declares during his life (viva voce or in writing) who shall be his heir.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'heir' does not necessarily imply children or nearest kin but whoever the ruler designates; an express declaration immediately invests the designated person after the predecessor's death. Hobbes cites Roman emperors' practice as example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession passes by not controlling a custom
rubrics_metrics.description: Where no testament is made, customary rule functions as evidence of the ruler's will: if custom dictates that nearest kindred or male kindred succeed, that custom establishes the right of succession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reasoning is that if the holder's will had been otherwise, he could easily have declared it; therefore failing to controvert an established custom is a natural sign of assent to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession by presumption of natural affection
rubrics_metrics.description: Absent testament or custom, succession is presumed to follow natural affection: first the ruler's own child (male or female), preferring males over females; next a brother rather than a stranger; nearer blood is preferred to more remote kin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption rests on human inclination to favor one's own children and nearer kin and on beliefs about fitness for labor and danger (Hobbes notes preference for males as 'naturally fitter' for such actions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarch may lawfully dispose succession to a foreigner
rubrics_metrics.description: It is lawful for a monarch to dispose of the succession by will or contract even to a foreign person or king of another nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objections about the inconvenience or oppression from foreign rule are attributed to unskillful governance rather than an inherent illegality of such disposition; examples (Romans granting privileges to conquered peoples; King James's attempt at union) are offered to argue that integration practices can mitigate those dangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominion acquired by generation (paternall) is by contract or consent, not mere begetting
rubrics_metrics.description: Parental (paternall) dominion over children is not derived simply from generation but from the child's consent — expressed or sufficiently evidenced — and can be disposed by contract between parents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no contract exists, dominion may lie with the mother (she first nourishes and has custody); if a child is nourished by another finder, dominion follows the nourisher. Precedent subjection of one parent to the other also determines who holds dominion (e.g., if mother subject to father, child is under father). Historical examples (Amazons) illustrate different results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education or nourishment confers dominion
rubrics_metrics.description: Where no contract exists, dominion is in the mother because she first nourishes; if she exposes the infant and another nourishes it, dominion is in the nourisher since preservation of life creates obligation of obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule ties dominion to the power to preserve or destroy life: one who preserves the child's life has the authority to command it; this grounds parental authority in practical dependency rather than mere generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominion by conquest (despotic) requires the consent/covenant of the vanquished
rubrics_metrics.description: Dominion acquired by conquest (despotic) is established when the vanquished, to avoid death or bonds, covenant by express words or other sufficient signs that they will allow the victor the use of their life and liberty; the conquest alone does not create lasting dominion without such consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quarter (surrender) without promise of life is only discretional; only when the victor trusts the captive with corporal liberty and obtains a covenant does servitude arise. The master then has authority over the servant and his possessions to the extent of the covenant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights and consequences of paternal and despotic dominion equal sovereignty by institution
rubrics_metrics.description: The rights and consequences of paternal and despotic dominion are the same as those of a sovereign by institution: the master/sovereign is sole judge, legislator, appoints magistrates, determines war and peace, and so forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes argues this equivalence to show that whether sovereignty arises by contract, generation (with consent), or conquest (with covenant), the resulting powers are identical in consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between a family and a kingdom
rubrics_metrics.description: A family, in respect of sovereignty, is like a little monarchy where the father or master is sovereign; yet a family is not a true commonwealth unless it has sufficient power (by numbers or opportunity) to defend itself without being subdued without hazard of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a group is too weak to defend itself, its members may lawfully act individually (flee, submit) in times of danger; the distinction matters for whether collective sovereignty exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign power ought to be absolute
rubrics_metrics.description: For the preservation of peace and the prevention of perpetual war, sovereign power—whether in one man or in an assembly—ought to be as great as possible and, practically, absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes supports this by reason (without adequate sovereign power perpetual war ensues) and by scriptural citations (Samuel, Solomon, Christ 'Give to Caesar'). He acknowledges objections (practical evils) but insists the greater evil is lack of sovereign authority. Practice in long-lived commonwealths shows subjects did not dispute sovereign power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated rights of the sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: The sovereign's rights include: power cannot be transferred without consent, cannot be forfeited, cannot be accused or punished by subjects; sovereign judges what is necessary for peace and doctrine, is sole legislator, supreme judge of controversies, determines times/occasions of war and peace, chooses magistrates and officers, and determines rewards, punishments, honour, and order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rights are presented as consequences of the institution of sovereignty and are defended by the same reasons given earlier for absolute rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty defined as absence of external opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty (freedome) properly signifies the absence of external impediments of motion; a free-man is one who is not hindered in those things which by his strength and wit he is able to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes emphasizes proper versus improper uses of 'liberty' (not applied to non-moving things), and gives examples (bodies restrained by walls or chains, water contained by banks). This technical definition underpins his later claims about subjects' liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty is consistent with fear and necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and necessity do not negate liberty: actions performed through fear (e.g., throwing goods overboard to save a ship) are voluntary and therefore the actions of a free man; likewise, voluntary actions have causes and can be seen as necessary when causes are traced, but remain instances of liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes uses analogies (water in a channel) and theological reconciliation (God's providence and human will) to argue for compatibility of liberty with determinism and fear-driven choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of subjects consists in what sovereign praetermits (liberty from covenants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects' liberty consists only in those actions which the sovereign has not regulated by covenant and law; within those unregulated domains subjects are free to act as their reasons suggest, e.g., buy/sell, choose abode, trade, institute children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes rejects demands for total exemption from law (which would let others be masters of one's life) and notes that civil laws are 'artificial chains' created by mutual covenants and upheld by the sovereign's sword. Thus liberty is limited to what remains after covenants/laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects' liberty compatible with unlimited sovereign power
rubrics_metrics.description: The liberty possessed by subjects does not abolish or limit the sovereign's absolute power; the sovereign's acts toward subjects cannot properly be called injustice because subjects are authors (via covenant) of those acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes argues that subjects authorize the sovereign by covenant, so sovereign actions are not unjust toward subjects except insofar as the sovereign remains subject to God's law; this is used to justify apparent tensions between absolute power and individual liberty.
